title: AlphaFold prediction of structural ensembles of disordered proteins
source: Science TLDR podcast episode 27 show notes
one_line: The authors introduce AlphaFold-Metainference, which uses AlphaFold-derived inter-residue distance predictions as restraints in physics-based molecular simulations to generate structural ensembles of intrinsically disordered proteins.
key_claims: AlphaFold distance predictions, despite training on folded proteins, carry usable information about disordered protein conformational ensembles.
Metainference simulations sample conformations consistent with AlphaFold distance maps, yielding ensembles rather than single structures.
Ensembles were validated against SAXS experimental data for 11 different disordered proteins.
Ensembles were further validated against detailed simulations of two neurodegeneration-associated proteins, Abeta and alpha-synuclein.
limitations: AlphaFold distance predictions extend only to about 22 angstroms, so longer-range contacts can be missed.
The 22 angstrom ceiling is especially limiting for very extended disordered regions.
Complete characterisation may still require integration with additional experimental techniques.
Validation rests on SAXS (a low-resolution ensemble-averaged observable) and on comparison to other simulations rather than direct high-resolution structures.
open_questions: Does the method reproduce residue-level observables (e.g. NMR chemical shifts, PREs, FRET distances) beyond ensemble-averaged SAXS?
Can the 22 angstrom prediction limit be overcome to capture long-range contacts in highly extended IDRs?
Why does a model trained on folded structures encode information about disordered ensembles, and does this reflect general principles of protein behaviour?
Do the predicted ensembles support actionable drug-discovery hypotheses for Abeta or alpha-synuclein?
